packets.key_finding: A field experiment nudge shrouding the minimum-payment autopay option cut minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, because nudged cardholders chose autopay amounts only slightly above the minimum.
packets.methodology: Field RCT on credit cardholders with six-month follow-up on autopay enrollment, payment amounts, and debt.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the 'defaults always help' premise in a comparable consumer financial product: shifting enrollment behavior did not change the underlying financial outcome, warning that our enrollment lift may not translate into more savings.
limitations: studies credit card debt paydown, not savings enrollment
does not test preset multiplier anchoring directly
packets.relevance_reason: Field RCT on consumer financial defaults showing enrollment change without behavioral improvement, directly informing the entry-mechanism and 'vanity metric' concern.
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics undermine automatic enrollment and auto-escalation effects: steady-state savings rates rise only 0.6% and 0.3% of income respectively, and only 40% of employees complete their first auto-escalation before opting out.
packets.methodology: Analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating job turnover, withdrawal upon separation, and auto-escalation opt-out over the medium/long run.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of the support team's objection: the enrollment lift from defaults shrinks sharply once turnover, withdrawal, and opt-out are accounted for, directly bearing on whether our enrollment numbers will be vanity.
limitations: 401(k) retirement accounts, not liquid consumer round-up savings
employer-plan turnover dynamics don't map onto an app-based product
packets.relevance_reason: Directly quantifies how much smaller default effects are over the medium/long run than initial estimates suggest, matching the brief's core persistence question.
packets.title: Smaller than We Thought? The Effect of Automatic Savings Policies
packets.abstract: Medium-and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and default savingsrate auto-escalation on retirement savings.Our analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporates the facts that employees frequently leave firms (often before matching contributions from their employer have fully vested), a large percentage of 401(k) balances are withdrawn upon employment separation, and many employees opt out of auto-escalation.Steady-state saving rates increase by 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% of income due to default autoescalation.Only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first escalation date, and more opt out later.

packets.key_finding: Default nudges have medium-to-large effects on consumer risk-taking, but a default nudge (especially one people refuse) lowers ratings of the wealth manager's honesty and advice quality, with framing of the ask also shifting invested amounts.
packets.methodology: Three experiments, including a large representative five-European-country sample (n=4207), on default-nudged financial investment decisions.
packets.why_it_matters: Provides EU consumer evidence that defaults can damage trust and perceived honesty — central to the dark-pattern risk the brief flags for the entry-mechanism decision — and shows framing of the contribution ask shifts amounts, relevant to how the multiplier field is worded.
limitations: financial-advisor context rather than a self-serve app
risk-taking investment decisions, not round-up savings specifically
packets.relevance_reason: Directly measures manipulation perception and framing effects of defaults among EU consumers in a financial-advice context, matching the brief's dark-pattern and framing concerns.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: Abstract-only: proposes a taxonomy and framework explaining when default effects persist or fade downstream, driven by the time course of choice/consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and salience of trade-offs.
packets.methodology: abstract-only theoretical synthesis and taxonomy of consumer default-effect literature, with a proposed research agenda.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives a conceptual map of exactly the persistence/disengagement question the brief raises and flags which factors (antecedent preferences, salience) predict whether enrolled-by-default users will disengage from the round-up feature.
limitations: theoretical taxonomy rather than an empirical estimate
no financial-product-specific data
packets.relevance_reason: Recent consumer-behavior framework directly targeting when and why default effects persist or decay over time, matching the brief's persistence question.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million tipping decisions finds 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of deviation cost and opt-out cost together, and a counterfactual added preset (15% alongside 20/25/30) captures 69% of achievable welfare gains at 5.4% revenue cost.
packets.methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on NYC taxi transaction data plus a stated-preference survey, with counterfactual menu simulations.
packets.why_it_matters: The deviation-cost/opt-out-cost decomposition and counterfactual preset-menu method is the specific technique for deciding which round-up multiplier value to pre-select and how many preset options to offer, transferring directly to the level-design decision.
limitations: taxi tipping, not financial savings
no data on longer-term persistence of chosen behavior
packets.relevance_reason: Explicit method transfer: its structural friction-decomposition and counterfactual preset-menu analysis is directly applicable to choosing and testing which multiplier to pre-select.
packets.title: Defaults and Decisions: Choice Architecture and Consumer Opt-Out
packets.abstract:
Why do consumers accept defaults (preset or suggested options)? This paper estimates a structural model that disentangles two frictions underlying default adherence: a deviation cost (the disutility when the final choice differs from the consumer’s ideal) and an opt-out cost (the effort to override the default). I estimate the model on 8.6 million tipping decisions from NYC Yellow taxi trips. A stated-preference survey identifies consumer tipping preferences independently of defaults. The central finding is friction complementarity: 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of both frictions; remove either friction and the remaining one alone cannot sustain default adherence. Structural parameters are approximately stable when default options change, consistent with defaults channeling behavior through choice frictions rather than reshaping preferences. Counterfactual analysis shows that adding a 15% tip option below the existing 20%–25%–30% menu captures 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
 This paper was accepted by Dube, Jean-Pierre, marketing.
 Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05272 .

packets.key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is highly insensitive even to substantial losses from the default option.
packets.methodology: Three natural/randomized experiments using random assignment to default options among Medicare beneficiaries.
packets.why_it_matters: Shows default stickiness can persist even when it hurts the enrollee, cautioning against assuming an opt-out default is automatically welfare-improving for disengaged consumers.
limitations: health insurance/drug benefit setting, not a financial savings product
low-income Medicare population differs from a general banking app user base
packets.relevance_reason: Strong evidence on persistence and insensitivity of passive default behavior, with distributional detail on low-income beneficiaries, relevant by analogy to sticky opt-out defaults.
packets.title: The Behavioral Foundations of Default Effects: Theory and Evidence from Medicare Part D
packets.abstract: We show in two natural experiments that default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization of low-income beneficiaries. The implications of this phenomenon for welfare and optimal policy depend on the sensitivity of passivity to the value of the default option. Using random assignment to default options, we show that beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive, even when enrolling in the default option would result in substantial drug consumption losses. A third natural experiment suggests that variation in active choice is driven by random transitory shocks rather than the inherent attentiveness of some beneficiaries.

packets.key_finding: Abstract-only synthesis: reviews how automatic enrollment and default investment options affect participation short- and long-term, including potential negative effects on participant engagement.
packets.methodology: abstract-only narrative overview of defined-contribution plan design literature.
packets.why_it_matters: Summarizes the engagement costs of passive enrollment across the closest analogous literature, giving context on disengagement risk, though the employer-trust mechanism it relies on does not carry over to a consumer app.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer app
abstract gives no explicit effect sizes
packets.relevance_reason: Recent comprehensive review of default/enrollment effects in the closest analogous (employer) literature, useful as synthesis context.
packets.title: Plan Design and Participant Behavior in Defined Contribution Retirement Plans: Past, Present, and Future
packets.abstract: This paper provides a state-of-the-art overview of defined contribution retirement plan design for academics, policy makers, and industry participants. I begin by considering the impact of basic plan design on participation rates, contribution rates, and portfolio choice, both overall and among employees with lower levels of financial literacy. Next, I consider the short-term and longer-term impacts of automatic enrollment and default investment options, including potential negative effects with respect to participant engagement. I also ask how the framing of plan features and plan communication can impact participant behavior. Finally, I examine recent plan changes including the integration of life annuities into retirement plans and target date funds (TDFs), managed accounts as alternatives to TDFs, emergency savings accounts, state-sponsored retirement plans, and national legislation like SECURE 2.0 that is intended to increase plan access and opportunities for employer matches.

packets.key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85%, but about 80% of participants anchored on the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, with half still at the default after three years.
packets.methodology: Administrative data analysis across three large firms tracking 401(k) participation and default anchoring over three years.
packets.why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that a pre-set default level strongly anchors the chosen contribution amount for years — the foundational evidence behind the brief's anchoring concern for the round-up multiplier.
limitations: employer 401(k) plan, not a consumer app
old, foundational study predating current fintech/regulatory context
packets.relevance_reason: Foundational study establishing that preset default levels anchor participant choices persistently, the classic evidence the anchoring literature builds on.
packets.title: Perspectives on the Economics of Aging
packets.abstract: In the last several years, many employers have decided to automatically enroll their new employees in the company 401(k) plan.Using several years of administrative data from three large firms, we analyze the impact of automatic enrollment on 401(k) participation rates, savings behavior, and asset accumulation.We find that although employees can opt out of the 401(k) plan, few choose to do so.As a result, automatic enrollment has a dramatic impact on retirement savings behavior: 401(k) participation rates at all three firms exceed 85%, but participants tend to anchor at a low default savings rate and in a conservative default investment vehicle.We find that initially, about 80% of participants accept both the default savings rate (2% or 3% for our three companies) and the default investment fund (a stable value or money market fund).Even after three years, half of the plan participants subject to automatic enrollment continue to contribute at the default rate and invest their contributions exclusively in the default fund.The effects of automatic enrollment on asset accumulation are not straightforward.While higher participation rates promote wealth accumulation, the low default savings rate and the conservative default investment fund undercut accumulation.In our sample, these two effects are roughly offsetting on average.However, automatic enrollment does increase saving in the lower tail of the savings distribution by dramatically reducing the fraction of employees who do not participate in the 401(k) plan.

packets.key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, passive automatic employer contributions raised savings substantially while active-choice tax subsidies mostly shifted assets between accounts (1 cent of new saving per $1 of subsidy); ~85% of individuals are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but strongly moved by automatic defaults, while active savers are wealthier and more sophisticated.
packets.methodology: Population-level administrative panel data from Denmark comparing responses to active-choice subsidies versus passive automatic contributions.
packets.why_it_matters: The classic evidence that passive defaults reach financially unsophisticated savers that active-choice policies miss — central to the brief's 'who is helped, who is hurt' question when weighing active choice against opt-out.
limitations: Danish retirement/taxable savings accounts, not a consumer app
outside the recency window the brief prioritizes
packets.relevance_reason: Foundational distributional evidence on who benefits from passive defaults versus active-choice policies, directly relevant to the brief's equity concern.
packets.title: Active vs. Passive Decisions and Crowd-Out in Retirement Savings Accounts: Evidence from Denmark *
packets.abstract: Abstract Using 41 million observations on savings for the population of Denmark, we show that the effects of retirement savings policies on wealth accumulation depend on whether they change savings rates by active or passive choice. Subsidies for retirement accounts, which rely on individuals to take an action to raise savings, primarily induce individuals to shift assets from taxable accounts to retirement accounts. We estimate that each $1 of government expenditure on subsidies increases total saving by only 1 cent. In contrast, policies that raise retirement contributions if individuals take no action—such as automatic employer contributions to retirement accounts—increase wealth accumulation substantially. We estimate that approximately 15% of individuals are “active savers” who respond to tax subsidies primarily by shifting assets across accounts; 85% of individuals are “passive savers” who are unresponsive to subsidies but are instead heavily influenced by automatic contributions made on their behalf. Active savers tend to be wealthier and more financially sophisticated. We conclude that automatic contributions are more effective at increasing savings rates than subsidies for three reasons: (i) subsidies induce relatively few individuals to respond, (ii) they generate substantial crowd-out conditional on response, and (iii) they do not increase the savings of passive individuals, who are least prepared for retirement.

packets.key_finding: Proposes and tests 'enhanced active choice' — a variant of active choice that highlights losses from the non-preferred option — as an alternative to automatic enrollment when defaults are infeasible or unethical, via field experiments in medication adherence.
packets.methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice against standard framing; abstract-only, health-care/medication-adherence context.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly informs the active-choice option for the entry decision: shows active choice can be strengthened by loss-framing rather than treated as a weaker compromise between opt-in and opt-out, which matters if the team wants active choice to capture more of the opt-out enrolment lift.
limitations: setting is medication adherence, not consumer financial products
no effect sizes for savings-specific behavior
field experiments are in health care, not fintech
packets.relevance_reason: One of the foundational papers introducing and testing active choice as a named alternative to opt-in/opt-out defaults, directly bearing on the entry-mechanism decision even though the domain differs.
packets.title: Enhanced active choice: A new method to motivate behavior change
packets.abstract: Abstract High rates of medication non‐adherence have significant public health and economic consequences. In other contexts such as savings behavior, opt‐out policies, in which the alternative preferred by the policy maker is made the default, have gotten great traction but may not be feasible in health care settings. After reviewing previous applications, we present a series of studies, including two field experiments, that test the effectiveness of an alternative, ‘active choice’ policy in which there is no default, but decision makers are required to make a choice (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, & Metrick, 2009; Spital, 1993, 1995). In addition, we propose and test a modified version of active choice, that we call ‘enhanced active choice’ that favors one alternative by highlighting losses incumbent in the in the non‐preferred alternative. We recommend Enhanced Active Choice as a complement to automatic enrollment or when automatic enrollment is infeasible or unethical.

alternates.key_finding: Auto-enrollment's gains in participation and contributions attenuate substantially between 12 months and 36 months, though it still reduces savings inequality; a life-cycle model implies a switching cost of about $250.
alternates.methodology: Analysis of over 100 US retirement plans and a UK panel, combined with a life-cycle consumption-savings model.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly answers the brief's persistence question: the enrollment/savings lift from defaults measured at signup does not hold up over 1-3 years, cautioning against reading initial enrollment numbers as durable.
limitations: retirement savings plans, not liquid consumer savings
life-cycle model calibrated to pension behavior
alternates.relevance_reason: Quantifies exactly how much default effects on savings shrink between 12 and 36 months, the timeframe the brief asks about.
alternates.title: Default Options and Retirement Saving Dynamics
alternates.abstract: Using data from over 100 US retirement plans and a representative UK panel, I document the impact of auto-enrollment (AE) on retirement savings at different horizons. I replicate the impact of AE on participation and contributions in the short run (at 12 months), but I show that these gains are attenuated over the medium run (at 36 months). At this longer horizon, the average savings increases are modest, though AE significantly lowers inequality in savings. To assess AE’s lifetime impact, I estimate a life cycle consumption-savings model that can fit the observed patterns with a switching cost of approximately $250, smaller than previous estimates. (JEL D15, G51, J26, J32)

alternates.key_finding: Opt-in take-up of a payroll-deduction short-term liquid savings account was under 0.7% of eligible employees, but among activators, 96% still had a balance and 87% received an automatic contribution at 12 months.
alternates.methodology: Field study of a short-term (liquid) savings program rollout across five UK firms, tracking activation and 12-month usage.
alternates.why_it_matters: The closest available product analog (liquid, opt-in short-term savings) shows opt-in enrollment is very low but engaged users persist strongly — directly informative for weighing the entry-mechanism trade-off even though it lacks an opt-out/active-choice comparison arm.
limitations: employer payroll-deduction context rather than a standalone consumer app
opt-in only, no opt-out or active-choice comparison arm
alternates.relevance_reason: Closest liquid, opt-in short-term savings analog with 12-month persistence data directly relevant to the entry decision, despite being employer-mediated.
alternates.title: Employer-Based Short-Term Savings Accounts
alternates.abstract: We study the introduction of a choice architecture design intended to increase short-term savings among employees at five U.K. firms. Employees were offered the opportunity to opt into a payroll deduction program that auto-deposits funds from each paycheck into a short-term savings account from which withdrawals are possible at any time. We find that employees who opted into the program kept using it. Among employees whose accounts were created early enough to be observed over the first 12 months after their account activation and who did not separate from employment during this period, 96% still had a balance greater than 1 and 87% received an automatic payroll contribution in month 12. However, product take-up was very low: no more than 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated an account. Opt-in access to short-term savings programs does not elicit widespread participation.

alternates.key_finding: Automatic enrollment into Germany's public pension raised participation by 23 percentage points, but most low-income individuals actively opted out, with the default effect stronger when incentives were higher and knowledge of enrollment status was lacking.
alternates.methodology: Natural policy experiment using linked administrative and survey data on nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees.
alternates.why_it_matters: Shows default enrollment gains can be substantially eroded by active opt-out and depend heavily on incentive salience and awareness, cautioning against assuming a stable, uniform enrollment lift.
limitations: public pension system, not a consumer banking app
low-income employee population differs from typical fintech users
alternates.relevance_reason: Quantified default effect with heterogeneity by knowledge/incentive and majority opt-out, informing the entry-mechanism decision.
alternates.title: Opt-in or Opt-out? The Power of Defaults in Pension Enrollment Choices
alternates.abstract: Default settings strongly increase pension enrollment, especially when savings incentives are high and choices are complex. We show that the effect is weaker when incentives are low, options are simple, and opting out is easy. We study the nationwide introduction of auto-enrollment for low-income employees in Germany's public pay-as-you-go pension system. We find that automatic enrollment raises participation by 23 percentage points, though most individuals actively opt out. Linking administrative and survey data shows that the default effect is stronger when enrollment incentives are higher and among individuals who lack knowledge of their enrollment status.

alternates.key_finding: Abstract-only: argues default enrollment raises short-term participation but induces passivity — low contribution rates, disengagement, account churn — undermining long-term welfare gains unless paired with escalation and re-enrollment mechanisms.
alternates.methodology: abstract-only narrative/policy discussion citing broader empirical literature on default enrollment.
alternates.why_it_matters: Explicitly voices the support team's disengagement concern about passively-enrolled users and proposes mitigations (auto-escalation, reminders) relevant to the level-setting decision.
limitations: employer retirement plan framing
perspective piece with no original data or effect sizes
alternates.relevance_reason: States the 'passive trap' critique of default enrollment that mirrors the brief's internal disagreement almost verbatim.
alternates.title: Default Enrollment in Retirement Plans: A Policy Nudge or a Passive Trap?
alternates.abstract: This article explores the policy effects and welfare impacts of "default enrollment" in the U.S. retirement savings system. As a "nudge" tool in behavioral economics, default enrollment significantly increases retirement plan participation through inertia and status quo bias, improving savings coverage and investment quality in the short term. However, extensive empirical research indicates that default enrollment can also induce behavioral inertia: employees tend to remain at low contribution rates, not actively manage their accounts, and even experience account churn. This "passivity" not only weakens long-term savings but also reflects a structural mismatch between employer incentives and employee benefits. Therefore, relying solely on increased participation rates is insufficient to demonstrate welfare improvements. This article advocates retaining the advantages of default enrollment while introducing automatic contribution increases, regular re-enrollment reminders, and financial education to mitigate long-term passive behavior and truly enhance individuals' retirement financial security.
alternates.venue: International Journal of Global Economics and Management

alternates.key_finding: A broad review of household financial behavior and behavioral-economics explanations for it, covering consumption/savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation and insurance, plus a survey of interventions (education, peer effects, product design, advice/disclosure, choice architecture, and price/quantity mandates) firms and governments use to shape those behaviors.
alternates.methodology: Narrative literature-review chapter synthesizing empirical regularities and behavioral models across household finance; abstract-only, no primary data or effect sizes given.
alternates.why_it_matters: Gives the broader theoretical backdrop for why choice-architecture interventions (defaults, product design) are expected to work in consumer financial contexts, useful for framing but not for sizing either the entry or level decision.
limitations: no quantitative effect sizes reported in the abstract
covers many domains at a survey level rather than round-up savings specifically
may lean heavily on employer-retirement literature within its household-finance framing
alternates.relevance_reason: Broad synthesis of behavioral household finance and choice-architecture interventions, useful as background context on the mechanisms the brief invokes, though not specific enough to move either design decision on its own.
alternates.title: Behavioral Household Finance
alternates.abstract: This chapter provides an overview of household finance. The first part summarizes key facts regarding household financial behavior, emphasizing empirical regularities that are inconsistent with the standard classical economic model and discussing extensions of the classical model and explanations grounded in behavioral economics that can account for the observed patterns. This part covers five topics: consumption and savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance. The second part addresses interventions that firms, governments, and other parties deploy to shape household financial outcomes: education and information, peer effects and social influence, product design, advice and disclosure, choice architecture, and interventions that directly target prices or quantities.
